qa_pairs.question:
In Rails' SQLite adapter, migrations that alter table structure (for example, a mere `add_foreign_key`) can wipe out a production SQLite table, as described in https://kyrylo.org/software/2025/09/27/a-mere-add-foreign-key-can-wipe-out-your-whole-rails-sqlite-production-table.html. Rails appears to already disable and re-enable the `foreign_keys` PRAGMA around table changes since https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/45881b0a64b4039e3b0d27e2c4d959dc2d744b9d, but the current ordering seems to be:

```
transaction do
  disable_referential_integrity do
```

I think it should instead be:

```
disable_pragma_foreign_keys do
  transaction do
    enable_defer_foreign_keys do
```

because SQLite documents that `PRAGMA foreign_keys` “is a no-op within a transaction; foreign key constraint enforcement may only be enabled or disabled when there is no pending BEGIN or SAVEPOINT,” while `PRAGMA defer_foreign_keys` is set per transaction and therefore has to be inside the transaction block. Should Rails change the SQLite table-recreation flow to disable `PRAGMA foreign_keys` outside the transaction, perform the change transactionally, and use deferred foreign keys inside the transaction?
qa_pairs.answer: Rails fixed this in PR #55907. The fix changes the SQLite table-recreation flow so foreign key enforcement is disabled before the table recreation process and re-enabled afterward. Because SQLite `PRAGMA foreign_keys` cannot be changed inside an active transaction, the correct sequence is to disable foreign keys outside the transaction, perform table recreation inside a transaction for atomicity, re-enable foreign keys afterward, and validate integrity with `PRAGMA foreign_key_check`.

qa_pairs.question:
In a Rails app using automatic DB switching (docs: https://guides.rubyonrails.org/active_record_multiple_databases.html#activating-automatic-role-switching) with the default resolver `ActiveRecord::Middleware::DatabaseSelector::Resolver` and context `ActiveRecord::Middleware::DatabaseSelector::Resolver::Session`, asset requests appear to get a `Set-Cookie` header in the response. I noticed this while investigating system tests not rendering flash messages correctly; it looked like race conditions between redirect requests and asset requests were overriding the cookie and removing the flash message. From debugging, it seems this happens because `ActiveRecord::Middleware::DatabaseSelector::Resolver::Session` reads `request.session[:last_write]`, causing the session to load, and perhaps `ActionDispatch::Session::CookieStore` then sends the cookie back in the response.

Steps to reproduce: I created this repo: https://github.com/EmilioCristalli/test_db_selector. It is a normal Rails app with a scaffold for one model (`Post`). The last commit on `main` has automatic DB switching enabled; moving one commit back to `9232d6768d` disables it. Open the root page (`posts#index`) and inspect asset requests such as `http://localhost:3000/assets/application-bfcdf840.js` in developer tools; with automatic DB switching enabled they include `Set-Cookie`.

Expected behavior: asset requests should not have a `set-cookie` header in the response, which is what appears to happen when automatic DB switching is not enabled.
Actual behavior: asset requests have a `set-cookie` header in the response.
System configuration: Rails 8.0.2.1, Ruby 3.4.5.

Is this a Rails/automatic DB switching bug, and is it expected that asset requests respond with a cookie in this setup?
qa_pairs.answer: This was treated as a Propshaft bug rather than expected behavior of Rails automatic DB switching itself. Propshaft was mounted inside the Rails routes, so asset requests were handled only after the normal Rack middleware stack had already run; that allowed middleware such as the database selector/session stack to touch the session and cause `Set-Cookie` on asset responses. The intended fix was to move Propshaft asset serving earlier in the Rack middleware chain, likely near `ActionDispatch::Static`. The issue was later fixed in rails/propshaft#249, which turned `Propshaft::Server` into proper middleware, and this Rails issue was closed as completed in that PR.

qa_pairs.question: In Rails translations, I want to interpolate safe HTML such as a `link_to` result without forcing the translation key itself to know whether the interpolation contains HTML. Currently I have to do either: ```erb <%= t(".text", insert: link_to(t(".insert"), root_path)).html_safe %> ``` or: ```erb <%= t(".text_html", insert: link_to(t(".insert"), root_path)) %> ``` But the `text_html` translation should not have to know whether `insert` contains HTML, and the Rails i18n guide does not explain a nice way to do this. Ideally Rails i18n would be aware of `SafeBuffer` and safely join content like this: ```yml text: some <> text with an %{insert} text_html: some <> text with an %{insert} insert: a link, properly escaping <> ``` ```erb <%= t(".text", insert: link_to(t(".insert"), root_path)) %> ``` Since `link_to` returns an `html_safe` string, the desired output would be: ```html some <> text with an a link, properly escaping <> ``` Is there a secure/simple way for Rails or rails-i18n to handle links and other safe content inside translations automatically using `SafeBuffer`, rather than requiring manual `html_safe` or `_html` keys for this case?
qa_pairs.answer: There was no landed Rails fix in this thread. A community member shared a SafeBuffer-aware translation interpolation implementation as a gist and said they would like similar behavior to become part of Rails or rails-i18n. The proposed direction is to preserve `html_safe`/SafeBuffer interpolations while escaping ordinary translation text and unsafe interpolation values, avoiding a blanket `.html_safe` on the whole translated string. However, this remained a proposal/community workaround; the issue was later closed as not planned.

qa_pairs.question:
In Rails ActiveRecord, calling `lease_connection` inside a transaction appears to leave a connection leased to the current thread after the transaction. Reproduction in `rails c`:
```ruby
puts "Before: #{ActiveRecord::Base.connection_pool.active_connection?}"
ActiveRecord::Base.transaction do
  ActiveRecord::Base.lease_connection
end
puts "After: #{ActiveRecord::Base.connection_pool.active_connection?}"
```
Expected:
```ruby
Before:
After: 
```
Actual:
```ruby
Before:
After: #<ActiveRecord::ConnectionAdapters::Mysql2Adapter>
```
This matters because our application mixes DB queries with slower HTTP requests and can hit MySQL connection limits; we need to return obtained DB connections to the pool before HTTP requests. We also saw it after adding `after_commit_everywhere` 1.6.0 to a Rails 7.2.2.1 app for `Sidekiq.transactional_push!`, where this leaks:
```ruby
class MyWorker
  include Sidekiq::Worker
  sidekiq_options queue: :default

  def perform; end
end

puts "Before: #{ActiveRecord::Base.connection_pool.active_connection?}"
ActiveRecord::Base.transaction do
  MyWorker.perform_async
end
puts "After: #{ActiveRecord::Base.connection_pool.active_connection?}"
```
The trace goes through:
https://github.com/sidekiq/sidekiq/blob/v6.5.12/lib/sidekiq/transaction_aware_client.rb#L16
https://github.com/Envek/after_commit_everywhere/blob/v1.6.0/lib/after_commit_everywhere.rb#L100
https://github.com/Envek/after_commit_everywhere/blob/v1.6.0/lib/after_commit_everywhere.rb#L111
https://github.com/Envek/after_commit_everywhere/blob/v1.6.0/lib/after_commit_everywhere.rb#L144
https://github.com/Envek/after_commit_everywhere/blob/v1.6.0/lib/after_commit_everywhere.rb#L172

System configuration: Rails 7.2.2.1 with Ruby 3.3.2, and Rails 8.0.2 with Ruby 3.4.4.

If `lease_connection` is designed to keep the connection leased until `release_connection`, how can I easily receive a connection without this sticky behavior in complicated nested code, e.g.:
```ruby
ActiveRecord::Base.transaction do
  do_call
end

def do_call
  # ActiveRecord::Base.connection or something else that will release connection after #transaction block
end
```
qa_pairs.answer:
Call `release_connection` when you are done with a leased connection, or only check out connections where needed using `with_connection`; nested `with_connection` gives you the same connection. The sticky behavior was by design to avoid breaking code expecting sticky connections, per PR #51192. You can also wrap the whole thing in `.with_connection(prevent_permanent_checkout: true)`.

```ruby
# call `release_connection` when you're done with a connection
ActiveRecord::Base.transaction do
  do_call
end
ActiveRecord::Base.release_connection

# or only checkout connections where you need them (nesting with_connection always gives you the same connection)
def do_call
  Base.with_connection do |c|
  end
end
```

qa_pairs.question:
In stripe-node with TypeScript, I used the `payment_method` attribute in `paymentIntents.create` and received this error:

`A token may not be passed in as a PaymentMethod. Instead, use payment_method_data with type=card and card[token]=tok_xxxx"`

So I tried to use `payment_method_data` and set the type as `card`:

`payment_method_data: { type: 'card', card: { token: 'tok_xxxxx' } },`

However, TypeScript reports that the interface `PaymentIntentCreateParams.PaymentMethodData` does not support the `card` type. Casting to `any` before passing to `.paymentIntents.create` works:

```ts
const stripeRequest = {
      amount: request.amount,
      currency: request.currency_code,
      application_fee_amount: 0,
      payment_method_types: ['card'],
      confirm: true,
      capture_method: 'manual',
      payment_method_data: { type: 'card', card: { token: 'tok_xxxx' } },
    };

    const res = await this._stripe.paymentIntents.create(stripeRequest as any);
```

Why does `PaymentIntentCreateParams.PaymentMethodData` not support `type: 'card'` with `card[token]`, and is there a supported way to do this?
qa_pairs.answer: The maintainers intentionally avoid typing the `card` hash because it would also include types for passing raw card details server-side, which requires a higher level of PCI compliance. Passing a token ID such as `tok_123` is supported, but Stripe views it as a temporary migration path rather than the canonical integration path; the recommended approach is to confirm the PaymentIntent client-side instead of server-side on creation. They do not plan to add types for this scenario, and casting as `any` is the workaround.

qa_pairs.question:
In a Stripe integration using `stripe-node` on the server and `@stripe/stripe-js` on the client, I create a server-side `Stripe.PaymentIntent` after validating a basket, then wanted to strip it down to the client-side `PaymentIntent` shape. The TypeScript errors I hit were:

```
Type 'import("stripe").Stripe.PaymentIntent.LastPaymentError' is not assignable to type 'import("@stripe/stripe-js").PaymentIntent.LastPaymentError'.
  The types of 'payment_method.customer' are incompatible between these types.
    Type 'string | Customer' is not assignable to type 'string'.
      Type 'Customer' is not assignable to type 'string'.ts(2322)
```

and:

```
Type 'string | PaymentMethod' is not assignable to type 'string'.
  Type 'PaymentMethod' is not assignable to type 'string'.ts(2322)
```

My reducer looked like this:

```
import { PaymentIntent } from '@stripe/stripe-js'
import Stripe from 'stripe'

// pi parameter should be of Stripe.PaymentIntent type - the server side PaymentIntent type definition
// But Stripe.PaymentIntent is incompatible with @stripe/stripe-js version of PaymentIntent.
// The below code results in Typescript error.

function reduceStripePIToPublishableKeyPermissions(pi: Stripe.PaymentIntent): PaymentIntent {
    return {
        id: pi.id,
        amount: pi.amount,
        client_secret: pi.client_secret,
        currency: pi.currency,
        description: pi.description,
        last_payment_error: pi.last_payment_error,
        next_action: pi.next_action,
        payment_method: pi.payment_method,
        payment_method_types: pi.payment_method_types,
        receipt_email: pi.receipt_email,
        setup_future_usage: pi.setup_future_usage,
        shipping: pi.shipping,
        status: pi.status,
        object: pi.object,
        canceled_at: pi.canceled_at,
        cancellation_reason: pi.cancellation_reason,
        capture_method: pi.capture_method,
        confirmation_method: pi.confirmation_method,
        created: pi.created,
        livemode: pi.livemode
    }
}
```

After reading more, it seems most frontend operations only need the client secret rather than other `PaymentIntent` attributes. I wanted to use the `PaymentIntent` as a single source of truth so displayed amount, currency, etc. match what the PaymentIntent will charge. Is Stripe's preferred approach to pass only the client secret from the server and have the client make additional Stripe queries as needed? Also, is there any built-in redaction function in `stripe-node` for turning a server-side `PaymentIntent` into a publishable-key-safe/client-side object?
qa_pairs.answer:
The server-side `Stripe.PaymentIntent` type is intentionally broader than the client-side `@stripe/stripe-js` `PaymentIntent` type. On the server, expandable fields such as `payment_method.customer` can be either an ID string or an expanded `Customer` object, while client-side Stripe.js cannot expose expanded customer data for security reasons, so its type only allows the safer client-side shape. This is why directly copying fields such as `last_payment_error` or `payment_method` can produce TypeScript incompatibilities, and `last_payment_error` may also contain sensitive information such as an entire Charge object.

There is no built-in redaction function in `stripe-node`, and the maintainer said they would not add one for now. If the frontend only needs to continue the payment, pass the `client_secret`; retrieving the PaymentIntent with a publishable key server-side would be equivalent to doing it client-side after returning the `client_secret`. If the frontend also needs fields such as amount or currency, the recommended approach is to define and return your own server-to-client object containing only those needed fields, rather than trying to cast a redacted server-side PaymentIntent into the Stripe.js PaymentIntent type.

qa_pairs.question: In stripe-node v8.131.1, I expected that setting `maxNetworkRetries` would result in retries when rate limited with HTTP 429 Too Many Requests, but in testing I noticed this is not the case. Would the Stripe team consider adding 429 as a condition that gets retried automatically in `_shouldRetry` (for example, `lib/StripeResource.js` around line 251 in v8.131.1)? I think the typical right thing to do when rate limited is automatic retries with exponential backoff, so it would be nice to have this in the built-in retry mechanism, though a higher max delay than 2s might also be useful for this use case.
qa_pairs.answer: Stripe does not automatically retry 429 errors because hitting rate limits usually indicates an issue in the application, such as making unnecessary requests, and SDK retries would hide the underlying problem. The maintainers expect most integrations not to hit rate limits; in test mode they cited a limit of 25 requests per second and suggested using mocks rather than hitting the API heavily in test suites. They also did not favor a `retryOnRateLimit` option for large clients, because rate-limit handling should be application-specific, with prioritization and alerting rather than blanket retries.

qa_pairs.question:
In urllib3/urllib3, using Python 3.12 in a virtualenv with `urllib3==2.6.2` from PyPI plus optional `h2==4.3.0`, I found several potential security/DoS issues and would like maintainers to triage them and advise on fixes/remediation.

### 1. Unlimited decompression can exhaust client memory (High)
- **Location:** `src/urllib3/response.py:619`-`src/urllib3/response.py:1110`
- **Impact:** When `Accept-Encoding` is enabled (default), `HTTPResponse.read()` always fully inflates compressed bodies without any upper bound on the decoded size. A malicious peer can send a very small gzip/brotli/zstd payload that expands to gigabytes, leading to client-side memory exhaustion or process termination, independent of the advertised `Content-Length`.
- **Details:** `_decode()` forces `max_length=-1` when `flush_decoder` is true (line 637) and directly feeds all incoming bytes to the decoder (line 641) while `read()` keeps appending to `_decoded_buffer` until the requested amount is satisfied or EOF (line 1097 onward). There is no limit tied to `Content-Length`, streaming hint, or caller-provided cap, so any compressed response is eagerly expanded into RAM.
- **Proof of Concept:**
  ```python
  import gzip, http.server, socketserver, threading, urllib3

  payload = gzip.compress(b"A" * (50 * 1024 * 1024))  # 50 MB after inflate

  class Handler(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
      def do_GET(self):
          self.send_response(200)
          self.send_header("Content-Encoding", "gzip")
          self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(payload)))
          self.end_headers()
          self.wfile.write(payload)
      def log_message(self, *args):
          pass

  server = socketserver.TCPServer(("127.0.0.1", 0), Handler)
  threading.Thread(target=server.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()

  http = urllib3.PoolManager()
  resp = http.request("GET", f"http://127.0.0.1:{server.server_address[1]}/")
  print(len(resp.data))  # prints 52428800, showing the inflated size held in memory

  server.shutdown()
  ```
  Increasing the payload size proportionally increases instantaneous memory usage in the urllib3 client process.
- **Recommendation:** Introduce configurable limits for the decoded body size, such as a cap based on `Content-Length`, a new `max_decoded_bytes` parameter, or stopping inflation once a threshold is hit, and allow streaming decoders to hand off chunks directly to the caller without buffering everything in `_decoded_buffer`.

### 2. `Retry-After` header induces unbounded client sleep (Medium)
- **Location:** `src/urllib3/util/retry.py:308-339`
- **Impact:** When `Retry.respect_retry_after_header` (True by default) is set, urllib3 trusts any `Retry-After` header and performs `time.sleep(retry_after)` with the parsed value. A malicious origin or intermediary can respond with `Retry-After: 31536000` to block the caller’s worker thread for a year, bypassing request-level timeouts and causing denial of service across thread pools.
- **Details:** `sleep_for_retry()` parses either a delta seconds or HTTP-date (lines 308-323) and, if present, unconditionally calls `time.sleep(retry_after)` (line 338) before reattempting the request. There is no upper bound, no linkage to the configured timeout, and no way to abort the sleep other than thread interruption.
- **Proof of Concept:**
  ```python
  import http.server, socketserver, threading, time
  import urllib3

  class Handler(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
      def do_GET(self):
          self.send_response(503)
          self.send_header("Retry-After", "5")  # attacker controls this value
          self.end_headers()
      def log_message(self, *args):
          pass

  server = socketserver.TCPServer(("127.0.0.1", 0), Handler)
  threading.Thread(target=server.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()

  retries = urllib3.util.retry.Retry(total=1, respect_retry_after_header=True)
  http = urllib3.PoolManager()
  start = time.time()
  try:
      http.request("GET", f"http://127.0.0.1:{server.server_address[1]}/", retries=retries)
  except urllib3.exceptions.MaxRetryError:
      pass
  print(round(time.time() - start, 2))  # ~5.0 seconds, equal to Retry-After header

  server.shutdown()
  ```
  Raising the header to hours or days will stall the thread for the same duration.
- **Recommendation:** Cap `Retry-After` sleeps to a configurable maximum, defaulting to a few seconds, or tie the sleep to the original request timeout; allow users to opt out or enforce asynchronous cancellation.

### 3. HTTP/2 responses are always fully buffered despite `preload_content=False` (Medium)
- **Location:** `src/urllib3/http2/connection.py:226-266` and `src/urllib3/http2/connection.py:324-347`
- **Impact:** The experimental HTTP/2 backend accumulates the entire response body in a `bytearray` (line 230) and materializes it into `HTTP2Response.data` regardless of the caller’s `preload_content` flag. There is no streaming API, so any large HTTP/2 download forces full buffering, opening the door to memory exhaustion when a remote server or CDN sends multi-GB responses. Dependent services expecting streaming semantics, such as `stream=True` in requests, silently lose back-pressure when HTTP/2 is enabled.
- **Details:** `HTTP2Connection.getresponse()` reads until `StreamEnded`, appending each `DataReceived` chunk to `data` (lines 248-255). The resulting bytes are stored in `_data` inside `HTTP2Response` (line 331), and methods such as `.stream()` are not implemented. The passed `preload_content` flag from `HTTPSConnectionPool.urlopen()` is ignored entirely for HTTP/2 connections.
- **Proof of Concept:**
  ```python
  import urllib3, urllib3.http2

  urllib3.http2.inject_into_urllib3()
  http = urllib3.PoolManager(headers={"accept-encoding": "identity"})
  resp = http.request(
      "GET",
      "https://nghttp2.org/httpbin/stream-bytes/10240",
      preload_content=False,
  )
  print(resp.version_string, len(resp.data))  # -> HTTP/2 10240
  urllib3.http2.extract_from_urllib3()
  ```
  Despite `preload_content=False`, the full payload is buffered in `resp.data`. Increasing the endpoint size quickly spikes RAM.
- **Recommendation:** Honor `preload_content=False` by exposing a streaming HTTP/2 response object, such as forwarding `DataReceived` frames to an iterator, or block HTTP/2 upgrades unless the caller explicitly opts in to buffering. At a minimum, document the limitation and provide safeguards, such as max buffered bytes, to prevent accidental memory exhaustion.

### 4. Redirect draining eagerly decompresses attacker-controlled bodies (High)
- **Location:** `src/urllib3/poolmanager.py:500`-`src/urllib3/poolmanager.py:503` and `src/urllib3/response.py:793`-`src/urllib3/response.py:801`
- **Impact:** When a response triggers a redirect, `PoolManager` always calls `response.drain_conn()` before following the `Location`. `drain_conn()` simply invokes `HTTPResponse.read()` with default arguments, which eagerly inflates any `Content-Encoding` on the response body. An attacker can reply with `302 Found`, a tiny compressed payload that expands to hundreds of megabytes, and a benign `Location`. The client must fully decompress the unused body before the redirect is honored, leading to CPU and memory exhaustion without the application ever touching the response object.
- **Details:** The redirect logic at `poolmanager.py:500-503` calls `response.drain_conn()` unconditionally. `drain_conn()` in turn calls `self.read()` (response.py:799-800), which performs the same unlimited decompression described in Finding 1. Because redirects are handled internally, even a single GET to an attacker-controlled URL can force the client to inflate arbitrary amounts of data just to reach the next hop.
- **Proof of Concept:**
  ```python
  import gzip, http.server, socketserver, threading, time, urllib3

  payload = gzip.compress(b"A" * (200 * 1024 * 1024))  # ~200 MB once inflated

  class Handler(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
      def do_GET(self):
          if self.path == "/next":
              self.send_response(200); self.end_headers(); self.wfile.write(b"ok")
              return
          self.send_response(302)
          self.send_header("Location", "/next")
          self.send_header("Content-Encoding", "gzip")
          self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(payload)))
          self.end_headers()
          self.wfile.write(payload)
      def log_message(self, *args): pass

  srv = socketserver.TCPServer(("127.0.0.1", 0), Handler)
  threading.Thread(target=srv.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()

  http = urllib3.PoolManager()
  start = time.time()
  resp = http.request("GET", f"http://127.0.0.1:{srv.server_address[1]}/")
  print(resp.status, resp.data, "elapsed", round(time.time() - start, 2), "s")
  srv.shutdown()
  ```
  Even though the redirect target is only “ok”, the client spends noticeable time decompressing the 200 MB payload. Scaling the compressed bomb quickly leads to out-of-memory conditions.
- **Recommendation:** Avoid decompressing or even reading redirect bodies entirely—most clients ignore them. At minimum, cap the number of bytes that `drain_conn()` will pull, both raw and decoded, or skip draining compressed redirect bodies by closing the socket instead of decompressing attacker data.

### 5. HTTP proxy redirects always drop `Authorization`/`Cookie` headers (Medium)
- **Location:** `src/urllib3/poolmanager.py:602`-`src/urllib3/poolmanager.py:616` and `src/urllib3/poolmanager.py:477`-`src/urllib3/poolmanager.py:487`
- **Impact:** When using a plain HTTP proxy with no CONNECT, urllib3 mis-identifies every redirect as “cross-host” because `ProxyManager.connection_from_host()` builds pools keyed on the proxy host (line 614). Consequently `conn.is_same_host(redirect_location)` always returns `False`, so the redirect logic strips every header listed in `Retry.remove_headers_on_redirect`—including `Authorization`, `Cookie`, and any user-provided entries—even if the redirect stays on the exact same origin. Authenticated HTTP workflows behind proxies therefore lose credentials or session cookies after the first redirect and often fall into infinite login loops.
- **Details:** For HTTP destinations, `connection_from_host()` ignores the target host and instead returns a pool for `self.proxy.host` (`poolmanager.py:614-616`). Later, `PoolManager.urlopen()` removes “unsafe” headers whenever `not conn.is_same_host(redirect_location)` (`poolmanager.py:477-487`). Because `conn.host` is the proxy, not the origin, this condition is always true and every redirect is treated as cross-origin.
- **Proof of Concept:**
  ```python
  import urllib3
  proxy = urllib3.ProxyManager("http://proxy.local:8080")
  conn = proxy.connection_from_host("example.com", 80, "http")
  print("pool host:", conn.host)  # -> proxy.local
  print("same host redirect?",
        conn.is_same_host("http://example.com/secure"))  # -> False
  ```
  The above means cookies/Authorization headers will be stripped before following even a relative redirect to `/secure`. Users behind mandatory HTTP proxies cannot stay authenticated on any site that issues redirects (OAuth, SSO, login flows).
- **Recommendation:** Track the original destination host separately from the proxy host when evaluating `is_same_host` for redirects, or short-circuit the removal logic when a forwarding proxy is in use so headers are only stripped when the destination host truly changes.

### 6. Enabling HTTP/2 globally makes proxy usage fail outright (Low)
- **Location:** `src/urllib3/http2/connection.py:94`-`src/urllib3/http2/connection.py:103` and `src/urllib3/http2/__init__.py:30`-`src/urllib3/http2/__init__.py:42`
- **Impact:** Calling `urllib3.http2.inject_into_urllib3()` replaces every `HTTPSConnection` with `HTTP2Connection`, which explicitly raises `NotImplementedError` whenever `proxy` or `proxy_config` is supplied. Any deployment that uses proxies, such as corporate networks or tests that rely on mitmproxy, immediately loses outbound HTTPS support once HTTP/2 is injected, effectively taking the client offline.
- **Details:** `HTTP2Connection.__init__` rejects all proxy kwargs (line 94) and the injector rewires `HTTPSConnectionPool.ConnectionCls` globally to `HTTP2Connection` (http2/__init__.py lines 30-36). Proxied requests therefore crash before any network traffic is attempted.
- **Proof of Concept:**
  ```python
  import urllib3, urllib3.http2

  urllib3.http2.inject_into_urllib3()
  proxy = urllib3.ProxyManager("http://127.0.0.1:3128/")
  try:
      proxy.request("GET", "https://example.com/", timeout=urllib3.util.Timeout(1))
  except Exception as exc:
      print(type(exc).__name__, exc)
  finally:
      urllib3.http2.extract_from_urllib3()
  # -> NotImplementedError: Proxies aren't supported with HTTP/2
  ```

Are these accepted as security vulnerabilities or bugs, and what fixes, workarounds, or existing tracking issues apply?
qa_pairs.answer: The maintainers asked that potential security vulnerabilities be reported privately through urllib3’s Security Policy. For the individual findings: unlimited decompression in the non-streaming API was already known but was not considered a vulnerability; users handling large, unknown-length, or untrusted responses should use the streaming API, and configurable maximum response-size limits were treated as a possible feature. The Retry-After unbounded sleep issue was a duplicate of #3743 and fixed in urllib3 2.6.3. HTTP/2 full buffering was acceptable to discuss publicly because HTTP/2 support is experimental/incomplete, and #3300 tracks streaming HTTP/2 response support. Redirect draining that eagerly decompresses attacker-controlled bodies was accepted as a valid security issue and fixed in urllib3 2.6.3 under GHSA-38jv-5279-wg99. HTTP proxy redirects dropping Authorization/Cookie headers was not accepted as a security issue because confidential information is not sent to third parties, but it was considered a bug. HTTP/2 proxy support is tracked by #3299.

For practicality purposes for anyone else hitting this error: a decent downgrade-avoiding workaround if you can control the SSL context passed into urllib3 is to just disable the `VERIFY_X509_STRICT` verification flag that is now set by default (courtesy @vstinner on https://github.com/python/cpython/pull/112389#issuecomment-2024625491 ):

```
>>> ctx.verify_flags & ssl.VERIFY_X509_PARTIAL_CHAIN

>>> ctx.verify_flags & ssl.VERIFY_X509_STRICT
<VerifyFlags.VERIFY_DEFAULT: 0>
>>> ctx.verify_flags & ssl.VERIFY_X509_PARTIAL_CHAIN
<VerifyFlags.VERIFY_DEFAULT: 0>
```

from here you can pass this `ctx` into a urllib3 PoolManager via:
```py
pool = urllib3.PoolManager(ssl_context=ctx)
```

```python3
import urllib3

with urllib3.PoolManager(assert_hostname="cs_sample_feed.s3.amazonaws.com") as http:

    print(resp)
```

In Terraform CLI v1.9.8, when I add the Terraform package to a Dockerfile, build the image, and push it to AWS ECR, AWS Security Inspector reports CVE vulnerabilities in additional libraries. Expected behavior is that AWS Security Inspector or other tools do not report CVE vulnerabilities.

Findings:

- CVE-2024-10006 - github.com/hashicorp/consul/api
- CVE-2024-10005 - github.com/hashicorp/consul/api

A vulnerability was identified in Consul and Consul Enterprise (“Consul”) such that using Headers in L7 traffic intentions could bypass HTTP header based access rules.

Installed version: v1.13.0
Fixed version: 1.20.1

- CVE-2024-51744 - github.com/golang-jwt/jwt/v4

golang-jwt is a Go implementation of JSON Web Tokens. Unclear documentation of the error behavior in `ParseWithClaims` can lead to situation where users are potentially not checking errors in the way they should be. Especially, if a token is both expired and invalid, the errors returned by `ParseWithClaims` return both error codes. If users only check for the `jwt.ErrTokenExpired ` using `error.Is`, they will ignore the embedded `jwt.ErrTokenSignatureInvalid` and thus potentially accept invalid tokens. A fix has been back-ported with the error handling logic from the `v5` branch to the `v4` branch. In this logic, the `ParseWithClaims` function will immediately return in "dangerous" situations (e.g., an invalid signature), limiting the combined errors only to situations where the signature is valid, but further validation failed (e.g., if the signature is valid, but is expired AND has the wrong audience). This fix is part of the 4.5.1 release. We are aware that this changes the behaviour of an established func

Installed version: v4.4.2
Fixed version: v4.5.1

Are these CVEs relevant to the Terraform CLI, and will Terraform update these dependencies?
qa_pairs.answer: The maintainer explained that the reported CVEs may exist in upstream dependencies, but they are not related to use of the Terraform CLI, so the scanner findings should not be treated as exploitable Terraform CLI vulnerabilities. qa_pairs.question:
In Kubernetes v1.35.0 (kind cluster created with kindest/node:v1.35.0; kubectl client v1.35.0, Kustomize v5.7.1, server v1.35.0), the kube-apiserver removes all managedFields from a custom resource when all of the following are true: the object has managedFields entries for multiple apiVersions, the CRD conversion webhook is temporarily unavailable/unreachable, and there is a write to the object via label or client-side apply. I expected the apiserver to return an error instead, because removing all managedFields can significantly affect later writes.

Reproduction uses these files:
- cr_cluster.yaml: https://github.com/user-attachments/files/25218546/cr_cluster.yaml
- cr_cluster_ssa.yaml: https://github.com/user-attachments/files/25218545/cr_cluster_ssa.yaml
- crd_cluster.yaml: https://github.com/user-attachments/files/25218548/crd_cluster.yaml
- crd_cluster_no_conversion.yaml: https://github.com/user-attachments/files/25218547/crd_cluster_no_conversion.yaml

Steps:
```bash
kind create cluster
```

Deploy the CRD without conversion configured so managedFields can be prepared with v1beta1 and v1beta2:
```bash
kubectl apply -f ./crd_cluster_no_conversion.yaml
```

Deploy and prepare the Cluster object:
```bash
kubectl apply -f ./cr_cluster.yaml
kubectl label clusters.v1beta1.cluster.x-k8s.io cluster-1  def=ghi --overwrite
kubectl label clusters.v1beta2.cluster.x-k8s.io cluster-1  abc=def --overwrite
kubectl get cluster cluster-1 -o json --show-managed-fields | jq '.metadata.managedFields' | grep apiVersion
```

Update the CRD to configure an unreachable conversion webhook:
```bash
kubectl apply -f ./crd_cluster.yaml
```

Trying to update the Cluster with server-side apply:
```bash
kubectl apply -f ./cr_cluster_ssa.yaml --server-side --field-manager=kubectl-ssa-test --show-managed-fields -o yaml
```
returns:
```text
Error from server: conversion webhook for cluster.x-k8s.io/v1beta2, Kind=Cluster failed: Post "https://webhook-service.system.svc:443/convert?timeout=30s": service "webhook-service" not found
```

Trying to update it with client-side apply:
```bash
kubectl apply -f ./cr_cluster_ssa.yaml --show-managed-fields -o yaml
```
returns an object whose managedFields are gone:
```yaml
apiVersion: cluster.x-k8s.io/v1beta2
kind: Cluster
metadata:
  annotations:
    kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration: |
      {"apiVersion":"cluster.x-k8s.io/v1beta2","kind":"Cluster","metadata":{"annotations":{},"name":"cluster-1","namespace":"default"}}
  creationTimestamp: "2026-02-10T19:15:47Z"
  generation: 1
  labels:
    abc: def
    def: ghi
    jkl: def
  name: cluster-1
  namespace: default
  resourceVersion: "632"
  uid: 4d46d2ab-ab60-4164-86a3-2c5f45576c02
```

The apiserver logs show:
```bash
kubectl -n kube-system logs -f kube-apiserver-kind-control-plane | grep "SHOULD NOT"
```
Output:
```text
E0210 19:17:25.150030       1 fieldmanager.go:155] "[SHOULD NOT HAPPEN] failed to update managedFields" err="failed to update ManagedFields (default/cluster-1; cluster.x-k8s.io/v1beta2, Kind=Cluster): conversion webhook for cluster.x-k8s.io/v1beta2, Kind=Cluster failed: Post \"https://webhook-service.system.svc:443/convert?timeout=30s\": service \"webhook-service\" not found" versionKind="cluster.x-k8s.io/v1beta2, Kind=Cluster" namespace="default" name="cluster-1"
```

Where is Kubernetes dropping managedFields in this failure path, and what would be an appropriate fix when the conversion webhook is unavailable?
qa_pairs.answer: The managedFields were being dropped in `UpdateNoErrors` in `staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/managedfields/internal/fieldmanager.go`, where the failure path called `RemoveObjectManagedFields(newObj)` after `f.Update(...)` failed. This could happen when managedFields conversion failed because the CRD conversion webhook was unavailable. The appropriate fix is to preserve the managedFields from the live object on this failure path, so the current update’s field changes may not be tracked but existing field ownership data is not silently lost. Only if the live/new object accessors cannot be obtained should Kubernetes fall back to removing managedFields. The issue was fixed after the report in PR #136949.

qa_pairs.question:
In Kubernetes kubelet v1.33.4 on AWS, when a Node object is deleted/recreated with the same name but a different UID, kubelet's `nodeinfomanager.go` / `tryUpdateCSINode` updates an existing CSINode but does not reconcile its `ownerReferences[0].uid`. The stale CSINode ownerReference can still point to the old Node UID, so Kubernetes garbage collection deletes the CSINode after the new kubelet starts, causing later volume attachment failures such as `csinode.storage.k8s.io "<node-name>" not found`.

Observed timing: kubelet started at `16:23:07.906`; GC of the CSINode happened at `16:24:03.591` for instance ID `i-019f660891131cc51`.

Expected behavior: when kubelet registers a CSI driver via `tryUpdateCSINode` and a CSINode object already exists for the node, kubelet should verify that the existing CSINode's ownerReference UID matches the current Node object's UID. If the UIDs do not match, kubelet should either delete the stale CSINode and recreate it with the correct ownerReference, or update the existing CSINode's ownerReference to reflect the current Node UID. This is the same class of bug as the Lease object issue fixed in #109777.

Minimal theoretical reproduction:
``` 
# 1. Identify your node name
NODE_NAME=$(kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')

# 2. Record the current Node UID and CSINode ownerReference UID (should match)
echo "Node UID:    $(kubectl get node $NODE_NAME -o jsonpath='{.metadata.uid}')"
echo "CSINode ref: $(kubectl get csinode $NODE_NAME -o jsonpath='{.metadata.ownerReferences[0].uid}')"

# 3. Delete the Node object (kubelet will re-register it automatically with a new UID)
kubectl delete node $NODE_NAME

# 4. Wait for the node to re-register
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready node/$NODE_NAME --timeout=120s

# 5. Compare UIDs again — they will NOT match
echo "New Node UID:        $(kubectl get node $NODE_NAME -o jsonpath='{.metadata.uid}')"
echo "CSINode ownerRef UID: $(kubectl get csinode $NODE_NAME -o jsonpath='{.metadata.ownerReferences[0].uid}')"

# 6. Wait for garbage collector to delete the stale CSINode (~30-60 seconds)
echo "Waiting for GC to delete CSINode..."
while kubectl get csinode $NODE_NAME &>/dev/null; do
  sleep 5
  echo "CSINode still exists, waiting..."
done
echo "CSINode deleted by garbage collector"

# 7. Confirm CSINode is gone and does not come back
sleep 30
kubectl get csinode $NODE_NAME
# Expected: Error from server (NotFound): csinodes.storage.k8s.io "<node-name>" not found

# 8. Create a PVC and pod to demonstrate the impact
kubectl apply -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: csinode-repro-pvc
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: csinode-repro-pod
spec:
  nodeName: NODE_NAME_PLACEHOLDER
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: busybox
      command: ["sleep", "3600"]
      volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /data
  volumes:
    - name: data
      persistentVolumeClaim:
        claimName: csinode-repro-pvc
EOF

# Patch in the actual node name
kubectl patch pod csinode-repro-pod --type=json \
  -p="[{\"op\":\"replace\",\"path\":\"/spec/nodeName\",\"value\":\"$NODE_NAME\"}]" 2>/dev/null || true

# 9. Observe the volume attachment failure
kubectl describe pod csinode-repro-pod | grep -A5 "Events"
# Expected:
#   Warning  FailedAttachVolume  attachdetach-controller
#   AttachVolume.Attach failed for volume "pvc-xxx" :
#   csinode.storage.k8s.io "<node-name>" not found

# 10. Cleanup
kubectl delete pod csinode-repro-pod --force --grace-period=0 2>/dev/null
kubectl delete pvc csinode-repro-pvc 2>/dev/null
```

Has this CSINode ownerReference reconciliation/GC deletion bug already been fixed, and if so in what Kubernetes version or PR?
qa_pairs.answer: The maintainer indicated this should already be fixed by Kubernetes PR #131098. They were pretty sure the fix is in Kubernetes v1.35, but noted it has not been backported to older Kubernetes versions, which may explain the report on v1.33.4.

rubric.text: A correct fix must prevent multiple ResourceClaims owned by the same pod from all being exempted from quota; when the pod has not identified its exact extended resource claim, only the first claim for that pod, ordered by creation timestamp and then name, may skip quota.
The exemption logic must still reject a ResourceClaim if the pod status explicitly identifies a different extended resource claim name.
The comparison of competing claims must be scoped to extended-resource claims in the same namespace owned by the same Pod UID, rather than globally or by pod name alone.
If the implementation cannot determine the other claims for the pod owner, it must fail closed by not granting the quota exemption.

qa_pairs.question: In Kubernetes 1.35, DRA extended resource quota verification in `getVerifiedPodUsage` appears to have a loophole: any number of `ResourceClaim`s can say they are owned by the same pod and set the same annotation, causing them to skip being counted by quota. A user could reproduce this by: 1) creating a pod to allocate the maximum number of GPUs allowed by quota and making it unschedulable in some way, 2) creating any number of `ResourceClaim`s pretending to be extended resource claims for that pod so they skip quota counting, and 3) creating other pods using those resource claims. This would let a user work around a system-admin-created quota for DRA extended resource devices. Is this issue fixed?
qa_pairs.answer: Yes. The DRA extended resource quota bypass was fixed in Kubernetes PR #135434. The fix prevents multiple annotated ResourceClaims owned by the same Pod from all skipping quota: when the Pod has not explicitly identified its extended resource claim, only the first owned extended-resource claim for that Pod, ordered by creation timestamp and then name, may receive the quota exemption. The logic also fails closed if it cannot verify the owned claims.

qa_pairs.answer: The issue was marked `/priority critical-urgent`. The root problem is not just validation; it is the allocator logic: it tries to create an IPAddress no matter what, exhausting all possibilities. Although API requests are bounded and eventually time out, this can DDoS the apiserver by keeping the apiserver and etcd spinning. Fix PR: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/135499
